title: Working for It
passage:
Enrichment at Vidmark Zoo is logged the way a diet is: what was offered, what was taken, and what it displaced. The keepers' first finding was that generosity fails. A puzzle box that gives up its almonds every time is worked hard for three days and then ignored, while a box that pays out on perhaps half of all attempts is still being turned over months later. The second finding was harder to act on. The devices that hold attention longest are the ones that most resemble the animal's foraging problem in the wild — bark to be stripped, a crevice too narrow for a whole hand — and those are also the ones that take a keeper twenty minutes to prepare each morning. The budget line is called enrichment; what it mostly buys is labor.
— Runa Kjellman, science desk

questions.prompt: What does the writer imply about the cost of enrichment at Vidmark Zoo?

options.text: That the objects used for enrichment tend to cost a zoo more than its visitors would ever guess.
That the expense lies mainly in the keepers' hours rather than in anything the zoo buys.
That money set aside for enrichment is quietly being spent on ordinary keeping duties instead.
That enrichment survives in a budget because it is cheaper than the alternatives a zoo would otherwise fund.

questions.rationale: TYPE-002 inference, one logical inch beyond the last two sentences. The passage never states a price for anything; it says the devices that work best 'take a keeper twenty minutes to prepare each morning' and closes on 'The budget line is called enrichment; what it mostly buys is labor.' Putting those together gives B: the real expense is staff time, not equipment. A = outside_knowledge with a plausible-sounding economics claim the text never makes — the only equipment the passage names is a puzzle box baited with almonds, and the wild problems it echoes (bark to be stripped, a narrow crevice) are found, not bought, so the passage points the other way. C = a misreading of the closing line as an accusation of diversion: preparing a puzzle box is enrichment work, not 'ordinary keeping duties', and the writer's tone is wry about where the money goes, not about whether it goes astray. D = a two-step leap into policy: the passage weighs devices against each other, never enrichment against some unnamed alternative, and offers no comparison of budgets at all. Hedge balance: A hedges with 'tend to' and B with 'mainly', so the qualified option is not uniquely the key; B is also the second-shortest option, not the longest.
